<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
I've read it. This follow-up settles several questions the earlier papers left open. On two of its own claims it is more confident than its analysis allows.

## What it reports

**Varden case-processing offices at 24 months**
- Output per FTE: −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2).
- A new hours measure, case-system log-in time, shows hours down 11%, against 12% on timesheets.
- Output per hour: +8.5% (3.4 to 13.8) using logs, +9.8% using timesheets. The comparable 9-month figure was +12.5%.
- Quality: unchanged.
- Sick days: −27%. Resignations: still roughly half the control rate.

**Mediation (registered at month 11)**
- Meetings explain 47% (28 to 66) of the per-hour gain.
- Fatigue explains 18% (2 to 34).
- 35% is unexplained.
- Baseline meeting time was similar in both arms (7.4 v 7.2 hours). It fell to 3.9 in treated offices and stayed at 7.0 in controls.

**Counter arm**
- Ended at month 12. Waits had reached 7.3 v 4.0 minutes.
- Restoring service would have needed 12% more staff, at about 9% more cost per contact.

**Unplanned observation**
- In month 15, two control offices audited and cut their meetings without changing hours. Their per-hour output then rose 4.1% against their own previous six months.

**Halden subset (14 of the 23 organisations with records)**
- 3 reverted, with output indices of 88–91 at reversion.
- The 11 that continued show record output of 96.8 and hours down 13.4%, an 11.8% per-hour gain. There is no comparison group.

**Bearing on earlier papers**
- The "entirely an artifact" claim is refuted.
- The meta-analysis's "no decay" rested on four studies, all uncontrolled and all using scheduled hours.
- In the one controlled long-run study, the gain fell by about a quarter.

**Arithmetic.** The figures check out: 0.966/0.88 → +9.8%, 0.966/0.89 → +8.5%, 96.8/0.866 → +11.8%, 34.9/40.3 → −13.4%. The mediation shares sum to 100%.

## What this settles

**"Entirely an artifact" is refuted, at least in this setting.** The trial meets the standards Varga and Holm themselves recommended: randomisation, record-based output, hours from system logs, two-year follow-up. It still finds a gain whose interval clearly excludes zero. A universal claim needs only one sound counterexample, and this is one. Whether the same holds elsewhere is a separate, open question.

**"No decay" is refuted as an inference.** The long-follow-up studies all had the design features the meta-analysis showed inflate effects. This confirms the concern I raised about the meta-analysis. In the one controlled study, the gain shrank.

**Coverage-bound work: the cost is now concrete.** The county ended the counter arm. Waits got worse after month 9, and restoring service would have cost about 9% per contact. Together with the meta-analysis's seven studies, this is closed.

**Two of my own earlier concerns are resolved:**
- *Baseline imbalance in meetings* (my point 5 on the 9-month report). Meeting time was balanced at baseline, so the reduction is attributable to the treatment.
- *Unrecorded work* (my point 2). The logs suggest it is small: about one percentage point of hours.

**Sickness and retention benefits persist at two years.** This holds under randomisation, which makes them the most robust non-output findings across all five papers.

## Where it says more than its analysis supports

**1. Part of the "decay" may be control offices improving, not treated offices fading.**

Two of the seven control offices cut meetings at month 15 and gained about 4% per hour. If the 24-month estimate covers months 16–24, that alone would pull the difference-in-differences down by roughly 2/7 × 4.1 ≈ 1.2 points. That is close to half the observed drop from 12.5% to 9.8%. The authors present the two facts separately and never connect them.

They should report treated and control trajectories separately, and the estimate with those two offices excluded. If the treated offices held steady, the fading story weakens. It would also mean that some of the treatment's benefit spread to the controls, which supports the meetings mechanism.

**2. "Confirms" is too strong for the mediation result.**

The test is genuinely stronger than the 9-month exploratory analysis. It was pre-registered, run at a new timepoint, and showed baseline balance. That earns more than "post hoc story". But four things limit it:

- **Mediators were not randomised.** Attributing 47% requires assuming no unmeasured confounding between meeting cuts and output. The limitations section concedes this; the summary's "confirms" doesn't.
- **There are 14 clusters, not "a larger sample of office-months."** Months within an office are not independent. An interval of 28–66% looks narrow for 14 clusters, so the authors should state how clustering was handled.
- **The decomposition may depend on order.** Cutting meetings probably reduces fatigue, so some of the fatigue share may belong to meetings, or the reverse. The authors should say how the joint pathway was apportioned.
- **The test may reuse exploratory data.** The hypothesis came from month-6 data. If the 24-month outcome is cumulative, it includes the months that generated the idea. The test is cleanest on data from after month 11 only.

Reasonable wording would be: meeting reduction is the largest *measured* pathway, supported by a pre-registered analysis, under standard mediation assumptions.

**3. The log-hours denominator changes what the mediation measures.**

Meetings take place outside the case system, so log-in time excludes them. That has two consequences:

- **Under timesheets,** a meeting cut can raise output per hour by moving time from meetings to cases.
- **Under log hours,** that route mostly disappears: more casework raises logged time and output together. What remains is a fragmentation effect, where fewer interruptions make each logged hour more productive.

So "meetings explain 47% of the gain in output per log-hour" is a specific claim about reduced fragmentation, not about reallocated time. That is interesting in its own right, but different from what most readers will take away.

There is also a numbers puzzle the authors should reconcile. Timesheet hours fell about 4.5 hours a week while meetings fell 3.5, implying non-meeting time fell only about 1 hour. Yet logged hours fell 11%, roughly 2.5–3 hours on a plausible logged baseline. Running the mediation on the timesheet denominator as well would show how much the result depends on the choice.

**4. The Halden subset is filtered three times, and "upper bound" is the wrong term.**

The organisations were selected three times over:
- they submitted records,
- they agreed to respond (14 of 23),
- they chose to continue.

The authors acknowledge the last two. And without a comparison group, the 11.8% is not strictly an upper bound: general economic conditions could have pushed output either way. "Likely optimistic" is accurate; "upper bound" is not. The authors should also confirm whether the 40.3-hour baseline belongs to these 11 organisations or is carried over from Varga and Holm's 27.

**5. One reversion doesn't fit the summary's framing.**

The marketing agency reverted citing client deadlines. That is discretionary, deadline-driven work, not coverage. Calling all three reversions "client-facing or coverage obligations" stretches the category to fit. This is a small but real case that the discretionary/coverage-bound binary doesn't capture, as the meta-analysis's limitations anticipated.

**6. The control-office meeting audit is light evidence, and the paper treats it that way.**

The evidence is two offices compared with their own previous six months, so regression to the mean and seasonality are both possible. As a rough check, the treated offices' 3.5-hour meeting cut accounts for about 4 points of gain (47% of 8.5%). Scaled linearly, the controls' 2.1-hour cut would predict about 2.4%, not 4.1%. The authors' framing, "suggests, without establishing", is right. The design question it raises, reorganisation alone versus reorganisation plus fewer hours, is the most useful next trial in this literature.

## The overall picture after five papers

**Found:**
- **Discretionary work.** A 20% scheduled cut produces an 11–13% cut in actual hours. Output per hour rises about 8–10%, and the gain lasts at least two years in a controlled setting, though smaller than at 9 months. Output per worker sits slightly below control: about −3%, with an interval from roughly −8% to +1%.
- **Coverage-bound work.** Output per worker falls about 9–11% and service worsens. Restoring it costs extra staff. This is consistent across studies, and one employer has ended a trial over it.
- **Headline pilot figures.** Gains above 20% come from scheduled hours, manager ratings and survivor samples.
- **Wellbeing.** Sickness falls roughly 27–31% and resignations roughly halve, persisting at two years.

**Supported but not settled:**
- **Mechanism.** Meeting reduction is the largest measured pathway and fatigue contributes less. The causal split rests on mediation assumptions, and a third of the gain is unexplained.

**Open:**
- **Fading or catch-up.** Whether the decline from 12.5% reflects treated offices fading or controls catching up.
- **The trajectory beyond 24 months.**
- **Reorganisation without the hours cut.** Whether it captures most of the gain, or whether the cut is what makes reorganisation happen and stick.
- **Other settings.** Generalisation beyond one public employer and self-selected private organisations, especially to manufacturing and shift work.

I can draft queries to the authors (trajectories, clustering in the mediation, the denominator), or write the consolidated found-versus-open summary across all five papers as a standalone document.
